question: How does Python's asyncio event loop work and what is a coroutine?
title: asyncio Event Loop and Coroutines
direct_answer: A coroutine is an async function that can pause at await points and yield control back to the event loop. The event loop is a single-threaded scheduler that runs coroutines — when a coroutine awaits something (I/O, a sleep, another coroutine), the loop switches to run other ready coroutines. asyncio.run() creates and runs the event loop. asyncio.create_task() schedules a coroutine to run concurrently. gather() runs multiple coroutines and waits for all.
interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of the async/await model — essential for modern Python backend roles using FastAPI or async Django.

sections.title: The event loop mental model
sections.content:
The event loop is a single-threaded scheduler. It maintains a queue of ready coroutines and runs them one at a time. When a coroutine hits an await expression, it suspends — the event loop marks it as waiting and runs the next ready coroutine. When the awaited operation completes (data arrives from the network, timer fires), the event loop marks the coroutine as ready again.

Coroutines are defined with async def and contain await expressions. await pauses the coroutine and yields control to the event loop. The event loop returns when the awaited thing is done. Unlike threads, there's no forced preemption — a coroutine runs until it explicitly awaits.

asyncio.gather(*coros) runs multiple coroutines concurrently and returns all results when all complete. asyncio.create_task(coro) schedules a coroutine to run 'in the background' and returns a Task object immediately.

Critical rule: blocking operations in async code block the entire event loop — all other coroutines are starved. Never call time.sleep() in async code (use asyncio.sleep). Never do file I/O with regular open() (use aiofiles). Never call synchronous database drivers (use asyncpg, aiomysql). Run blocking operations in a thread pool with asyncio.to_thread().

sections.title: asyncio patterns
sections.content:
import asyncio
import aiohttp

# Basic coroutine
async def fetch_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(f'/api/users/{user_id}') as resp:
            return await resp.json()

# Run from sync code
result = asyncio.run(fetch_user(1))

# Concurrent execution — much faster than sequential awaiting
async def fetch_all(user_ids: list[int]) -> list[dict]:
    # Sequential — waits for each before starting next
    # results = [await fetch_user(uid) for uid in user_ids]  # slow

    # Concurrent — all start at once, gather waits for all
    results = await asyncio.gather(*[fetch_user(uid) for uid in user_ids])
    return list(results)

# create_task for fire-and-forget or background work
async def main():
    task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_user(1))
    task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_user(2))
    # Tasks are now running concurrently
    user1 = await task1
    user2 = await task2

# Running blocking code in a thread (don't block the event loop!)
import time

async def safe_blocking():
    # WRONG: time.sleep(1) blocks the entire event loop
    # RIGHT: run in thread pool
    result = await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 1)  # Python 3.9+

# asyncio.sleep yields to event loop (correct)
async def countdown(n: int) -> None:
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):
        print(i)
        await asyncio.sleep(1)  # yields to event loop each second

sections.title: asyncio rules
items: await pauses coroutine, yields to event loop — other coroutines run
gather() for concurrent execution — not sequential awaits in a loop
create_task() schedules coroutine immediately — doesn't block
NEVER block the event loop: no time.sleep(), no sync I/O
asyncio.to_thread() for blocking code in async context (Python 3.9+)

seo.metaDescription: Understand Python asyncio: event loop single-threaded scheduler, coroutines with async/await, gather for concurrency, and never blocking the event loop.

speakable_v2.hook: The event loop is a single-threaded scheduler — when a coroutine awaits, it steps aside and lets other coroutines run.

beats.content: The event loop runs coroutines one at a time. When a coroutine hits await, it suspends and the loop picks up the next ready coroutine. When the awaited operation finishes, the coroutine is marked ready again. No threads, no locks needed — cooperative switching at every await.

Sequential awaits in a loop is slow — you wait for each before starting the next. gather() starts all coroutines at once and waits for all to finish. That's the pattern that makes async HTTP calls fast.
The critical rule: never block the event loop. time.sleep() freezes all coroutines. Use asyncio.sleep() instead. For unavoidable blocking code, use asyncio.to_thread() to run it in a thread pool.

speakable_v2.cap: One blocked coroutine blocks everything. If you see a latency spike with asyncio, look for a synchronous database call or file read inside an async function.
